title: Bars and Baby Stars
caption: The barred spiral galaxy NGC 7541, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
celestial: NGC 7541 · constellation Pisces · about 110 million light-years away (source figure)
credit: ESA/Hubble & NASA, A. Riess et al.

recognition.text: ESA/Hubble Picture of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: The NASA/ESA Hubble Space Telescope captured NGC 7541, a barred spiral galaxy in the constellation Pisces. It lies about 110 million light-years away and forms a pair with its nearby companion, NGC 7537.

In a barred spiral, the spiral arms wrap around a bright center crossed by a bar of gas and stars. The bar is thought to stir up the central region and feed processes such as star formation and active galactic nuclei, which might otherwise never begin or might have stalled. As many as two-thirds of spiral galaxies may have bars, the Milky Way among them.
NGC 7541 forms stars faster than usual. That supports the idea that bars act as stellar nurseries, gathering gas and funnelling it inwards where it can build new stars.
scale: Using the source's listed field of view (2.65 x 1.94 arcminutes) and distance (110 million light years), the frame spans roughly 85,000 × 62,000 light-years. Its light set out about 110 million years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: The image combines observations from Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys and Wide Field Camera 3 in visible and near-infrared light, from 350 nm to 1.6 μm. The color assigned to each filter isn't published.
understand.eye: Part of the data is near-infrared light, which the eye cannot see, and Hubble's exposures gather far more light than an eye can.
